b.overview: Sit and grab two awful crimps, to the left of the line Leave it to Jesus. Erosion has worn away the holds below the stand start's slot jug, so this is punchy, difficult and body-type dependent. Strong climbers seldom finish it.

a.name: Last Days Extension
a.overview: Beyond the chains of Last Days, two fun bulges, then a headwall, lead to just under the rim. The style differs but is no harder than the lower route, and a 70m rope still lowers you down. Clip the new upper anchor, step right then back up-left, into a crack that bulges steeply in a small corner facing right. A further bulge reaches a blocky ledge; one tricky move gives a lovely crack to the anchor. Stay on line, since rock beside it may be loose.
a.location: Anchor chains sit over Last Days, just beneath the canyon rim.

a.name: Lion Zion (Extension)
a.overview: For those with energy and quickdraws left after Lion Zion, carry on above its anchors through seven additional bolts on chalk-free nubbins and crimps, steepening near the top. Grades 11a from Gumby, harder (11b/c) from Zebra Direct. An 80m rope is needed; rappel to the Lion Zion anchors, then once more to reach the ground. Carry 22 draws, including alpine-length ones to cut drag.

b.name: Pelican French Kiss
b.overview: A smooth, gently angled conglomerate slab runs to a roof that is simple to avoid via easy 5.4 jugs, reaching the slender summit. The top has no bolts: sling the summit or place gear in boulders below it. A wedged orange Trango cam remains stuck. Descend by the route or the gully on the south side.
b.location: Starts between Sun Kissed and the crag holding Never Been Kissed.

a.name: The Hole Bat-hang Variation
a.overview: A playful alternative start for The Hole. Sit facing opposite to the normal way, swing both feet well above your head into the boulder gap, and begin hanging by your knees. The finish matches The Hole's usual exit.
a.location: Found at the same boulders as The Hole.

a.name: Peawabe Spiral
a.overview: Easy adventure outing that also suits a solo ascent. A brief boulder move from the ground gains the broad tilted ramp circling the foot of Peawabe; many spots allow stepping onto it. Follow the ramp rightward, winding around the tower counter-clockwise, with nothing harder than third class. Retrace the line to descend.
a.location: South flank of Peawabe Rock, the standout formation along Indian Ridge.

b.name: Peawabe Spiral, Direct Variation
b.overview: Takes the pair of clear cracks straight up Peawabe, also called squaw rock. Likely harder than the spiral line, yet protection is solid for most of it; only the final 5 m or so is truly runout. Hangers without chains form the summit anchor. A 70m rope reaches to within about 3 m of the ground when rappelling beside the route; downclimb the rest. Take care for falling rocks while retrieving the rope.
b.location: At the obvious crack of roughly 8 m on the uphill flank of the Hitchhiker's Thumb; approach details are under Indian Ridge.

a.name: Don's Dream

a.location: the leftmost line on the slab

a.name: Scratch
a.overview: Directly upward from a sturdy hanging block with solid footholds, just right of where the neighbouring traverse finishes. Effectively an eliminate, so for the full line keep your hands off anything left of the crack. It is contrived, yet that is how the line is usually climbed.

a.name: Spliff
a.overview: Tall, fun and mentally taxing. Tall and enjoyable, with a mental edge. Left of Roach, northern face of the boulder it shares with Scratch: grab the good jug there, go directly up, and stay composed.

b.name: Toilet Bowl Traverse
b.overview: A left-to-right sweep across the full bowl, although the opposite direction is probably feasible. High-quality for what it is and a sensible area warm-up, if somewhat contrived, and nicer than the neighbouring lines on this block.

b.name: Spray Against the Undertow
b.overview: Every bit the classic that the stand start is. Hands begin in a sloping left hueco and a sidepull undercling at thigh height. Odd, deceptive sequences take you past the boobs, then up the arete; picking the obvious sequence often makes it feel harder. Height and reach matter somewhat.
b.location: Next to Silly Steep Mantle, on its right.

a.name: South Side (Hogsback)
a.overview: The most-climbed route on Oregon's highest peak, starting from the lodge on its south flank and following the ski area, then a snow ridge between steaming fumaroles, to the summit ridge. Most of it is a long snow walk, but the last thousand feet is steep, exposed snow above a bergschrund with rockfall and icefall from the surrounding cliffs. It is usually done in one long day with a very early start.
a.beta: From the top of the ski area, climb the snowfield toward the prominent dark buttress of Crater Rock and pass it on its east (climber's right) side, above the sulfur-smelling fumarole area of Devil's Kitchen, to reach the Hogsback, a narrow snow ridge on the north side of Crater Rock that leads up toward the summit cliffs. Put crampons on at its base. The Hogsback ends below a bergschrund that crosses the slope; how it is passed changes through the season. Above it, the Pearly Gates are a narrow, Y-shaped gully through the rime-coated rock straight ahead; they are the most direct finish but are often icy or melted out. The more common finish now is the Old Chute: from the low point on the Hogsback crest, drop slightly to the north side and climb a broad steep face into a narrowing chute through the summit cliffs, steepening to around 45° before topping out on the summit ridge. Walk the ridge east to the true summit, staying well back from cornices overhanging the north face.
a.approach: From the parking lot at Timberline Lodge, head north past the lodge to the marked climbers' trail, which follows the east edge of the ski runs. The Silcox Hut is roughly a thousand feet above the start. Keep climbing on the east side of the groomed runs and out of the way of snowcats and skiers, up past the top of the Palmer lift at about 8,500 ft. Above that, continue up the snowfield toward Crater Rock, passing the steaming fumarole area of Devil's Kitchen and the Hot Rocks, and swing around the east side of Crater Rock to the base of the Hogsback.
a.descent_text: Descend the way you came, most parties reversing the Old Chute facing into the slope, then down the Hogsback and around Crater Rock to the ski area and back to the lodge. In poor visibility, a compass bearing that does not account for the fall line will pull descending parties off to the southwest onto the Zigzag Glacier and toward Mississippi Head, or southeast toward White River Canyon; carry a planned bearing or track and follow it carefully.

waypoints.name: Timberline Lodge
waypoints.directions: From US 26 just east of Government Camp, turn north on Timberline Road and drive about 6 miles to the parking lots at Timberline Lodge. Fill out the free self-issued wilderness permit at the climbers' register in the Wy'east Day Lodge before starting. An Oregon Sno-Park permit is required to park from November through April.

waypoints.name: Mount Hood
waypoints.directions: Take the climbers' trail on the east edge of the ski runs past the Silcox Hut and the top of the Palmer lift at about 8,500 ft. Continue up the snowfield toward Crater Rock, past Devil's Kitchen and the Hot Rocks, and swing around its east side to the base of the Hogsback. Follow the snow ridge to the bergschrund, climb the Old Chute to the summit ridge, and walk east to the top.

b.name: South Side Route
b.overview: The quickest and busiest line on the mountain, a plain and fairly short climb up the south slope. Slow parties tend to bottleneck beneath the bergschrund, and newcomers should not underestimate it despite its easy reputation.
b.approach: Start at Timberline Lodge and walk the marked path up the right side of the ski area, avoiding the ground under the lifts. Head straight up toward the right side of Crater Rock. The Devil's Kitchen is a large flat area on the way and the usual rest stop. Above it is the Hogsback, the saddle between Crater Rock and the summit; fumaroles near it can release toxic gas.
b.descent_text: Descend the way you came up, taking care because conditions can change quickly.

a.name: East Ridge
a.overview: A well-established trail leads from the parking lot, meeting the PCT after 1.1 miles. Continue on the climbers trail past a second PCT junction (heading north) by staying straight. About 3 miles of good flowing trail precede the technical ground, where rocky footing, big step-ups and big drops lead to the East Ridge. Plod up the ridge to the last 600ft, a scree (or snow) slope ending at a large, pointed summit.
a.approach: From the trailhead parking lot a good trail runs about a mile to the first Pacific Crest Trail junction. Stay on the McLoughlin climbers trail, go straight past a second PCT junction that leads north, and follow smooth trail for a few miles before the footing turns rocky, with large step-ups. The well-worn trail leads to the East Ridge itself, and the final slope to the pointed summit is scree or snow.

a.name: South Ridge (from Summit Lake)
a.overview: The shortest and most popular way up Diamond Peak: a mellow stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail from Summit Lake, then a steep, cairned climbers' path up the broad south ridge to a false summit. From there a narrow, exposed volcanic spine with a few rock spires leads to the true summit, the only part of the day that needs hands.
a.beta: Leave the Pacific Crest Trail at a large open, rocky viewpoint marked by cairns and follow the climbers' path straight uphill. It climbs steeply through timber, where large rocks give handholds, then breaks out at treeline onto open ground with views south to Summit Lake, Cowhorn Mountain and Mount Thielsen. Above treeline the path gives way to a steep slope of loose talus and cinder that leads directly to the false summit; trekking poles help here. At the false summit, stow the poles. The true summit lies about 0.4 mi north along the summit ridge, roughly 500 ft higher: the spine looks thin from the false summit but is mostly 3 to 4 ft wide, with a few rock spires that you climb around or over using your hands, and steep drops on both sides. The summit itself is large and flat, with views north to Waldo Lake, the Three Sisters and Mount Bachelor. If the ridge does not feel right, the false summit is a worthwhile objective on its own.
a.approach: From the Summit Lake trailhead, walk north on the Pacific Crest Trail. This section is gentle, gaining only about 1,000 ft in about 4.5 mi as it winds through forest past several small ponds. At about 3.1 mi, pass a junction with trails to Rockpile and Marie lakes (left) and toward Fawn Lake (right); stay on the PCT. Roughly 1.3 mi farther, where the trail bends at a large open area with rocks and a big view, a cairned climbers' path leaves the trail to the west and heads uphill. This is where you leave the PCT.
a.descent_text: Reverse the route: back along the summit ridge to the false summit, down the loose talus slope, and down the climbers' path to the PCT, then south to Summit Lake. Below the talus it is easy to keep going straight down the fall line, which puts you out near Marie Lake instead of on the climbers' path; watch for the cairns where the path re-enters the trees, or follow your own recorded track from the ascent.

waypoints.name: Summit Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Highway 58 near Crescent Lake, take Forest Road 60 about 7 miles west, then continue on Forest Road 6010 about 6.5 miles west to Summit Lake. Forest Road 6010 is rough and not maintained for low-clearance vehicles; high clearance is strongly recommended.

waypoints.name: Diamond Peak
waypoints.directions: Walk north on the Pacific Crest Trail, passing the Rockpile and Marie lakes junction at about 3.1 mi. About 1.3 mi farther, at a large open rocky viewpoint, take the cairned climbers' path west steeply up through the trees. Above treeline, climb loose rock and cinder to the false summit, then follow the narrow, exposed spine about 0.4 mi north to the summit.

b.name: Southwest Ridge
b.overview: Easiest access when snow closes the Summit Lake road, and a handy way in for skiers after the bowls beneath the top. The trailhead at Pioneer Gulch gives a round trip of 7.5 miles and gains somewhat over 4000 feet. Hike until the trail joins the one named for Diamond Peak, then go directly uphill bearing climbers left to the southwest ridge. Stay on it until it merges with the south ridge, and continue to the top.
b.approach: Start at the Pioneer Gulch trailhead and follow the Pioneer Gulch Trail until it meets the Diamond Peak Trail. Leave the trail there and head straight uphill, trending toward climber's left, until you reach the southwest ridge. In winter, with the Summit Lake road shut, this is the easiest line to reach.
